genxml.title: INT2 local interrupt controller and 8254 timer block (Indigo, R3000 and R4000 boards)
genxml.doc: The Indigo's interrupt multiplexer: two local interrupt status and mask registers, the VME interrupt status and masks, a five-bit port register that also acknowledges the vertical-retrace latch, a timer acknowledge strobe and an 8254 timer block. Offsets are from the INT2 base, physical 0x1fb801c0 on both the R3000 and R4000 Indigo boards, and name the byte a big-endian CPU addresses: each register is one byte on a 4-byte stride and sits in the low byte lane, so a little-endian CPU addresses the same register 3 bytes lower (0x1fb801c0 for local 0 status). Names follow the shipped IRIX header for the R4000 Indigo and, for the 8254, the standard part; NetBSD's names for the same offsets are in the page. Grades: established means read in full in the R4000 Indigo kernel object or the 4.0.5D PROM (the README cites the addresses) or stated by a public header; inferred means a reasoned reading; unknown means nothing shipped settles it. Nothing was measured on a board. The prose is in devices/int2/README.md and the interrupt routing table in the R4000 Indigo platform directory.

struct.name: LOCAL0_STATUS
struct.doc: Raw state of the eight local 0 sources, one bit each, high while the source asserts. It is not gated by the mask: the PROM clears both masks and then reads status, and IRIX ANDs status with the mask in software. Bit layout is the LOCAL0 constants. A qtest can discriminate: a write has no effect; the bit follows the source signal.

struct.name: LOCAL0_MASK
struct.doc: Enables local 0 sources toward the CPU. A one bit lets the source raise the local 0 output. All eight bits read back what was written: the PROM writes 00 aa cc f0 ff 55 33 0f in turn and compares. A qtest can discriminate: byte write then read of 0xaa and 0x55.

struct.name: LOCAL1_STATUS
struct.doc: Raw state of the eight local 1 sources. Same rules as local 0 status. With all masks clear the PROM expects bits 0, 2, 3 and 4 to read zero and tolerates bits 1, 5, 6 and 7.

struct.name: LOCAL1_MASK
struct.doc: Enables local 1 sources toward the CPU. All eight bits read back.

struct.name: VME_STATUS
struct.doc: VME interrupt request levels 1 to 7 in bits 1 to 7 (inferred from the header names; no shipped R4000 Indigo code reads it for VME). Bit 0 is read by the GR2 retrace handler as the vertical-retrace status, active low (the header says 'no interrupt' when set): the handler polls it up to ten times 1 microsecond apart. NetBSD names this offset the map status register of the Indy's INT3 and gives it a different meaning.

struct.name: VME0_MASK
struct.doc: Which VME levels may raise local 0 bit 7. The IRIX routine that targets an I/O interrupt at the CPU sets bit n in this register. The PROM never reads this register back.

struct.name: VME1_MASK
struct.doc: Which VME levels may raise local 1 bit 3. The PROM writes 0x5a and checks the read-back, so all eight bits hold.

struct.name: PORT_CONFIG
struct.doc: Five-bit read/write port at the offset NetBSD calls the map polarity register on the Indy generation. The header calls it the LED and serial-port configuration register. Bits 1 and 2 are the RTS lines of serial ports 0 and 1 (the serial driver sets and clears them to switch the port between RS-232 and RS-422 modes); bit 3 is the vertical-retrace interrupt latch control; bit 4 is named power in the header. The PROM writes 0x16 during start-up. The header also names bits 1 to 3 as LEDs on the R4000 board and bit 0 as a cache parity flag; which role a bit plays on which board, and the LED polarity, are not settled.

struct.name: TIMER_ACK
struct.doc: Write-only strobe. Writing 1 clears the timer 0 interrupt latch, 2 clears timer 1. IRIX acknowledges timer 0 with 1 and timer 1 with 2; the PROM writes 3 at start to clear both. Writing zero bits has no effect. A qtest can discriminate: timer 0 interrupt line drops after a write of 1 and timer 1 stays asserted.

struct.name: ERROR_STATUS
struct.doc: No R4000 Indigo kernel object or the PROM touches this offset. NetBSD defines it for the Indy generation, where Linux calls it reserved on INT2. Nothing shipped for the Indigo reads it.

struct.name: TIMER0
struct.doc: 8254 counter 0 data, one byte at a time per the control word. Its output is the timer 0 interrupt (CPU IP4). IRIX loads it with 50 after control word 0x34, giving 100 Hz from the 5 kHz counter 2 output.

struct.name: TIMER1
struct.doc: 8254 counter 1 data. Its output is the timer 1 interrupt (CPU IP5), the profiling and fast clock. IRIX loads it with 5000 divided by the wanted rate, MSB shifted down, after control word 0x74.

struct.name: TIMER2
struct.doc: 8254 counter 2 data. Its output clocks counters 0 and 1 (NetBSD's header states this; IRIX's counter 0 and 1 divisors only make sense with it). IRIX counts 200 into it; the PROM reuses it as a 100 Hz reference with count 10000 and latches it with control word 0x80.

struct.name: TIMER_CONTROL
struct.doc: 8254 control word. The R4000 Indigo kernel and the PROM only write it. Standard 8254 layout; the values seen are 0x34, 0x74 and 0xb4 (counter 0, 1, 2 in mode 2 with LSB then MSB), 0x32, 0x72 and 0xb2 (mode 1) and 0x80 (latch counter 2) and 0xb8 (counter 2 mode 4).
